## Lewis Acid Supported Nickel Nitrenoids

Cristin E. Juda1Δ, Claire E. Casaday1Δ, Ryan M. Clarke1, Nicholas P. Litak1, Brandon M. Campbell1, Tieyan Chang2, Shao-Liang Zheng1, Yu-Sheng Chen2, Theodore A. Betley1*

ΔThese authors contributed equally.

Dr. C. E. Juda, C. E. Casaday, Dr. R. M. Clarke, N. P. Litak, B. M. Campbell, Dr. S.-L. Zheng, Dr. T. A. Betley 1Department of Chemistry and Chemical Biology

Harvard University 12 Oxford St, Cambridge, MA 02138 Email: betley@chemistry.harvard.edu Dr. T. Chang, Dr. Y.-S. Chen 2ChemMatCARS Beamline, The University of Chicago Advanced Photon Source, Argonne, IL 60429 Supporting information for this article is given via a link at the end of the document.

Abstract: Metalation of the polynucleating ligand F,tbsLH6 (1,3,5- C6H9(NC6H3-4-F-2-NSiMe2tBu)3) with two equivalents of Zn(N(SiMe3)2)2 affords the dinuclear product (F,tbsLH2)Zn2 (1), which can be further deprotonated to yield (F,tbsL)Zn2Li2(OEt2)4 (2). Transmetalation of 2 with NiCl2(py)2 yields the heterometallic, trinuclear cluster (F,tbsL)Zn2Nipy (3). Reduction of 3 with KC8 affords [KC222][(F,tbsL)Zn2Ni] (4) which features a monovalent Ni center. Addition of 1-adamantyl azide to 4 generates the bridging μ3–nitrenoid adduct [K(THF)3][(F,tbsL)Zn2Ni(μ3–NAd)] (5). EPR spectroscopy reveals that the anionic cluster possesses a doublet ground state (S = ½). Cyclic voltammetry of 5 reveals two fully reversible redox events. The dianionic nitrenoid [K2(THF)9][(F,tbsL)Zn2Ni(μ3–NAd)] (6) was isolated and characterized while the neutral redox isomer was observed to undergo both intra- and intermolecular H-atom abstraction processes. Ni K-edge XAS studies suggest a divalent oxidation state for the Ni centres in both the monoanionic and dianionic [Zn2Ni] nitrenoid complexes. However, DFT analysis suggests Ni-borne oxidation for 5. Introduction

Metal ligand multiple bonds (MLMBs) play an important role in group transfer catalysis as critical intermediates.[1-8] To make synthetic MLMB complexes more reactive, chemists have targeted high-spin electronic configurations for the MLMB unit or through binding Lewis acids to the multiply bonded fragment. Whereas electronic population of antibonding orbitals destabilizes MLMB complexes by diminishing the bond’s covalency,[9-16] Lewis acid coordination to the MLMB decreases the covalency to the redox-active metal when the multiply bonded functionality serves as a Lewis base.[17-24] We propose a combination of these two approaches via incorporation of Lewis acids into a cluster core to stretch the primary redox pair (i.e., the redox active transition metal and multiply bonded ligand) beyond what is possible with traditional MLMB formulations.

To generate clusters incorporating Lewis acids, we undertook stepwise metalation of the polynucleating ligand (F,tbsL)H6 ((F,tbsL)H6 = [1,3,5-C6H9(NC6H3-4-F-2-NSiMe2tBu)3]) (Scheme 1, top left). Herein, we report on the synthesis and reactivity of a heterotrinuclear cluster (F,tbsL)Zn2Ni(py) that features a single redox-active transition metal, supported by two Lewis acidic Zn2+ centers. The similarly sized Zn2+ centers serve to stabilize the electrostatic interactions between the [Zn2Ni] core to a nitrenoid fragment (e.g., NR) while the Ni acts as the unique redox active center. Indeed, the clusters support nitrenoid capture to afford the corresponding nitrenoid adducts with Ni–N bond lengths (2.002(5) Å) well in excess of terminal (1.642(7)–2.732(4) Å)[25-37] or Lewis acid supported (1.897(2) Å).[23]) MLMBs, exceeding even cluster imidos (i.e., NR2–) with Ni in similar oxidation states.[38-39]

The previously reported trinucleating ligand platform (tbsL)H6[40] was modified to incorporate a fluorine atom on each ortho-

phenylenedianilide subunit, located para to the basal nitrogen, providing a 19F NMR handle sensitive to the local chemical environment of each ligand subunit. The ligand (F,tbsL)H6 = [1,3,5- C6H9(NC6H3-4-F-2-NSiMe2tBu)3] was synthesized in a modified version of the procedure previously reported for (tbsL)H6.[41]  The details of the ligand synthesis can be found in the SI.

## Results and Discussion

A stepwise approach to metalation of the (F,tbsL)H6 platform was used to promote compositional homogeneity of the target heterobimetallic complexes.[42] Thus, we began with installation of the Lewis acidic Zn2+ centers, followed by a metathesis route to install the redox active M2+ center (Scheme 1). The comparable size of Zn2+ to the redox-active first-row transition metal of interest and its relative inertness to oxidation or reduction make it an ideal candidate as the Lewis acid within the trinuclear clusters described herein.[43] Metalation of (F,tbsL)H6 with two equivalents of the dibasic reagent Zn(N(SiMe3)2)2 in benzene at 110 °C (Scheme 1) yielded the dinuclear complex (F,tbsL)H2Zn2 (1) which features two ligand N–H units into which the last metal is installed. Crystals suitable for single-crystal X-ray diffraction (SCXRD) were grown from a concentrated diethyl ether solution of 1 at –33 °C and confirmed the incorporation of two Zn2+ cations into the ligand platform (Figure S52).

Deprotonation of the two remaining N–H units in 1 was achieved by addition of two equivalents of LiN(SiMe3)2 in thawing benzene (Scheme 1). Consumption of 1 was determined by the disappearance of resonances associated with 1 in the 1H and 19F NMR spectra with the appearance of a new diamagnetic species. Crystals suitable for SCXRD were grown from a concentrated diethyl ether solution of the product, confirming the deprotonation of 1 to afford the dilithio complex (F,tbsL)Zn2Li2(OEt2)4 (2). The solid-state structure of 2 reveals one Li+ cation is contained within the trinuclear core and coordinated to one diethyl ether molecule; whereas the second Li+ cation lies outside the trinuclear pocket and is coordinated to one ligand fluorine and three diethyl ether molecules (Figure 1a). Transmetalation of 2 with one equivalent of NiCl2(py)2 in a thawing benzene solution afforded a deep purple colored solution. The reaction completeness was gauged by the disappearance of 2 and concomitant appearance of a new diamagnetic species in the 19F NMR spectrum which featured three distinct resonances (19F δ/ppm: –108, –116, –120). The reaction mixture was filtered to remove insoluble materials and evaporated to dryness. Crystals were grown by cooling a concentrated solution of the product in diethyl ether to –33 °C. SCXRD on crystals of the product confirmed formation of a trinuclear cluster (Figure 2b). Each of the three metals in the product (F,tbsL)Zn2Ni(py) (3) reside in distinct coordination environments. One metal site is coordinated in an approximate T-shaped planar geometry supported by two F,tbsL basal nitrogens and one pyridine molecule. This metal is also engaged in an interaction with the ipso-carbon of one of the orthophenylenedianilide arms of the ligand. The average M–M distance within the core is 3.077(6) Å, exceeding the sum of van der Waals radii (3.02 Å).[43] Ultraviolet/visible/near infrared (UV/vis/NIR) absorption spectroscopy of 3 reveals max = 512 (4600), and 647 nm (2800 M–1cm–1) (Figures S20-22). The determination of metal identities within the cores of 3 and the derivatives thereof is complicated by the similar atomic scattering factors of Ni and Zn[44] when irradiated with in-house X-ray sources (Mo or Cu Kα radiation). Therefore, the heterometallic clusters were analyzed via X-ray fluorescence (XRF) spectroscopy to assess their Zn:Ni ratios. The ratio of the areas under the Kα curves (resulting from an L-shell to K-shell relaxation) in the emission spectrum for each metal were compared to a calibration curve to identify the Zn:Ni ratios for each cluster.[40] The ratio of Zn to Ni of 3 was revealed to be 2:1 in

accord with its expected formulation. To gain further insight into the metal substitutional preferences within the core, crystallographic data for 3 and its derivatives were modeled by treating each metal site as a Zn/Ni disordered pair and refining their occupancies with the following variables: the sum of Ni and Zn occupancies at each site is 1, and the total Zn:Ni = 2:1 in the core. For 3, the final occupancies show that each site is occupied almost exclusively by Zn or Ni (see Figure S55 for exact occupancies). The metal distributions of 3 and its derivatized complexes, will be further probed using advanced crystallographic studies and presented in a subsequent report.

Treatment of 3 with one equivalent of KC8 and one equivalent of 2,2,2-cryptand (C222) to sequester the K+ cation yielded an anionic heterotrinuclear complex. Analysis of the reaction product by 1H and 19F NMR spectra reveal the consumption of diamagnetic 3 and the appearance of a new species featuring paramagnetically shifted resonances (1H δ/ppm: 89 to –41; 19F δ/ppm: –114 (br), –122). Crystals suitable for SCXRD were grown from a concentrated solution of the reaction product in diethyl ether. The solid state structure confirmed the assignment as [C222(K)][(F,tbsL)Zn2Ni] (4), in which the metal-bound pyridine has been expelled from the cluster and the F,tbsL ligand is arranged in a nominally C3-symmetric fashion about the trinuclear core (Figure 2c). Each position within the trinuclear core was modeled as Zn/Ni disordered pairs whose occupancies across the three positions sum to 2 and 1 respectively, in accordance with the XRF determined Zn:Ni ratio (1.90:1). The average metal–metal distance within the core of 4 is 2.688(2) Å, which is decreased relative to that observed in 3 (3.077(1) Å). We attribute this decrease to the expulsion of the side-bound pyridine ligand. The K+ cation, despite encapsulation by 2,2,2–cryptand, maintains an interaction with one ligand fluorine atom. EPR studies of 4 in frozen 2- methyltetrahydrofuran solutions at 77 (Figure 3b, top), 40 (Figure S26), and 4 K (Figure S27) revealed a rhombic S = ½ signal (g = 2.390, 2.230, 2.090) similar to the values from our previously reported Ni1+ complex on a dipyrrin platform.[34] Additionally, the spectrum features hyperfine coupling to an 14N nucleus on the g3 tensor, with (A)14N = 14 G. indicating spin delocalization  onto a ligand-based anilido nitrogen. UV/vis/NIR absoprtion spectroscopy of 4 reveals max = 575 nm (500 M–1cm–1) (Figures S29-31).

Crystallization from a concentrated solution of the product in diethyl ether at –33 °C yielded X-ray quality crystals. The solid state structure revealed a μ3–bound nitrenoid species [K(THF)3][(F,tbsL)Zn2Ni(μ3–NAd)] (5) (Figure 2c). The elongated nature of the M–NAd bonds for 5 prompted us to investigate its electronic structure. SQUID magnetometry revealed a spin ground state of S = ½ for 5 (ΧMT = 0.4 cm3K/mol, 50 K, Figure S38, expected value for S = ½; XMT = 0.375 cm3K/mol). Moreover, the EPR spectrum of 5 in frozen 2-methyltetrahydrofuran solutions at 77 (Figure 3a, bottom), 40 (Figure S35), and 4 K (Figure S36) reveal a rhombic signal  (g = 2.485, 2.231, 2.050) consistent with an S = ½ species. Interestingly, the spectrum features hyperfine from two different nuclei with different hyperfine coupling constants. One hyperfine coupling constant ((A)14N = 11 G) is similar to the ligandbased nitrogen coupling observed in 4, while an additional hyperfine signal ((A)14N = 23 G) is similar to those resported for terminal Ni– Nimidyl species,[27;34-36] though lower than those reported for a terminal iron-imidyl with 14N-hyperfine contributions in excess of 100 G.[47]

Nitrenoid adduct 5 was also examined by cyclic voltammetry, revealing two quasi-reversible events at –1.63 V and –0.62 V (vs. Cp2Fe+1/0) (Figure 3b). The voltamogram for 5 indicates that 1 e– oxidation and reduction of 5 should be accessible. Indeed, reduction of 5 with KC8 (1 equiv.) leads to the formation of the dianionic [K2(THF)9][(F,tbsL)Zn2Ni(μ3–NAd)] (6) whose paramagnetically shifted

19F NMR spectrum (Figure  2c, bottom) is consistent with the triplet configuration (S = 1) suggested by magnetometry (ΧMT = 0.99 cm3 K/mol, 50 K, Figure S46, expected value for S = 1; XMT = 1.00 cm3K/mol).  The dark red product was characterized with UV/vis/NIR absorption spectroscopy revealing peaks at max = 515 (1300 M–1cm–

1) and 1004 nm (760 M–1cm–1) (Figures S47-49). The molecular structure of 6 was determined by SCXRD (Figure 2b). The crystal structure adopts the hexagonal space group P63, where the asymmetric unit contains 1/3 of the molecule. Therefore the metal site was modeled with a fixed occupancy of 67% Zn and 33% Ni. The [Zn2Ni(μ3–NAd)] core of 6 is isostructural to that of 5. Each M–NAd

distance of 6 is 1.981(4) Å, which decreased from the observed average M–NAd distance in monoanionic 5 (2.002(5) Å).

Given the mild redox potential and electrochemical reversibility observed for the oxidation of 5, we also canvassed the oxidation of 5 with chemical oxidants. Oxidation of 5 with [Fc][PF6] in thawing THF generates two new products as ascertained by 19F NMR spectroscopy. Storage of a concentrated solution of the oxidation products in diethyl ether at –33 °C afforded crystals suitable for SCXRD. Despite the apparent reversiblility of the redox couple in the voltammogram of 5, the crystals obtained from the chemical oxidation of 5 (precipitated from Et2O over 12 h at –33 C) reveal a gross structural rearrangement of the F,tbsL about the cluster core (Figure 4). Furthermore, the nitrenoid functionality (NAd) changes hapticity from μ3 in 5 and 6 to μ2 in the products, accompanied by a net H–atom transfer to the nitrenoid fragment. Two species were identified by SCXRD; one whereby an intramolecular H–atom transfer from the cyclohexane backbone of the F,tbsL ligand occurs (7, Figure 4b),  and another where the H–atom source is intermolecular and one orthophenylenedianilide unit is oxidized to its semiquinonate form (8, Figure 4c) as determined by comparing the observed Caryl–N bond lengths (Figure S74) with 5 (F,tbsL C–Cavg (1.390(2) Å) and 6  (F,tbsL C– Cavg (1.375(4)Å)) (Figure S71-S72) which are consistent with each subunit maintaining its dianionic state.[48] In both species, the molecular structures are best refined with Ni residing in the oxidized ortho-phenylenedianilide unit and the μ2–NHAd unit bound to two Zn centers. Given the apparent reversibility of the electrochemical oxidation, the products of chemical oxidation are likely not representative of the kinetic product of oxidation. We propose the kinetic oxidation product is either Ni or nitrenoid NAd–borne which tautomerizes to the species observed crystallographically. Attempts to intercept the kinetic product of oxidation prior to tautomerization with nitrenoid acceptors (e.g., PPh3, styrene, tBuNC, 1,4- cyclohexadiene) were unsuccessful.

Following the successful syntheses of the mono- and dianionic [Zn2Ni] nitrenoids, we sought to better understand the electronic description of the nitrenoid ligand and the redox active Ni center. We considered three possible electronic descriptions for the S = ½ 5: (1) the Nin+ site is in the 3+ oxidation state, and (NAd) is a dianionic imido (Scheme 2a);[6;8] (2) the Ni site is 2+ and (NAd) is a monoanionic imidyl (Scheme 2b);[10;33-35]  or (3) the Ni site is monovalent and (NAd) binds as a neutral nitrene (Scheme 2c).[15;49] We rule out F,tbsL orthophenylenedianilido oxidation given (vide supra), though the F,tbsL ligand N–donors may contribute to the electroactive orbitals. Reduction of 5 yields the dianionic, spin triplet (S = 1) 6, for which we propose the following possible oxidation state descriptions: (1) Ni2+(NR2–); (2) Ni+(2NR1–); or (3) Ni0+(3NR). To better understand the relative oxidation states of the Ni centers in 5 and 6, we conducted single crystal Ni K-edge X-ray absorption studies (XAS). The pre- and rising-edge absorption features of 6 were

compared with those of 5. Both spectra feature a pre-edge absorption at 8.33 keV, and a slight shoulder along the rising edge (Figure 3c). Comparison of metal oxidation state between different complexes via XAS is difficult due to the importance of geometrical parameters in the scattering of incident radiation.[50] The exquisite structural similarities between 5 and 6 (Figure 2), however, allow us to directly compare the degree of Ni oxidation in each complex via their X-ray absorption spectra. The well-overlaid Ni K-edge data indicate that the formal oxidation assignments of the Ni centers in 5 and 6 are indistiguishable. As the nitrenoid fragment of 5 is poorly described as a nitrene (based on previously mentioned reactivity studies), we favor the assignment of 5 as a divalent nickel coupled to an imidyl (Scheme 2b); and 6 as a divalent nickel imido (Scheme 2a) as being most consistent with the spectroscopic data presented. Future studies will include N K-edge XAS to evaluate the hole character on the proposed imidyl moiety of 5,[51] as well as replacement of the adamantyl fragment with alternative substituents to probe the effects of sterics and electronics on the electronic structure and reactivity of the Lewis acid supported nitrenoids.

Lastly, DFT analysis was performed on complexes 4–6 using ORCA (version 5.0.4)[52-53] to ascertain which elements feature in their frontier molecular orbitals. Geometry optimizations were performed using the experimental (crystallographic) structures as the input geometries using the TPSSh functional.[54-55] Broken symmetry calculations on 5 afforded the same solutions as the corresponding unrestricted calculations performed (see SI for details). Subsequent single-point energies were calculated at the TPSSh-D4/def2- TZVPP[56] level of theory and the quasi-restricted orbitals (QRO) for compounds 4–6 were used to examine their frontier orbital makeup.

The computation results indicate considerable spin-delocalization onto the various N-donors from the Ni frontier orbitals, giving rise to the hyperfine contributions seen in the low temperature EPR (Figure 3a). For example, complex 4 reveals significant mixing of the ligand basal anilido group with the formally NiI center as illustrated in the SOMO shown in Figure 5a. The mixing of both the Ni 3d (69%) and N 2p (6.7%) indicates why N–hyperfine coupling ((A)14N = 14 G) is observed in the 77 K EPR spectrum obtained for 4.

Examination of the redox isomers 5 and 6 revealed contributions from Ni and N-donors from both the nitrenoid and templating (F,tbsL) ligands. Thus, the DFT analysis suggests assignments of monoanionic 5 and dianionic 6 and NiIII and NiII imido formulations, respectively, in contrast to the XAS analysis (vide infra) which indicates an indistinguishable oxidation level between the two redox isomers. The nitrenoid (NAd) orbital parentage predicted for 5 (and 6) is less significant than values reported for the more covalent, terminally bound nitrenoid complexes.[27;34-36;47] While the dominant orbital parentage for MO299 (depopulated upon oxidation of 6 to generate 5) is largely Ni-centred, the cumulative natural charge for the nitrenoid functionality changes upon reduction from 5 (–1.341) to 6 (–1.534) while the Ni charge remains nearly constant (5, 1.241; 6, 1.269). The natural spin population changes from 5 to 6 do show increases on both the nitrenoid (5, 0.075; 6, 0.197) and Ni centers (5, 0.924; 6, 1.440) resulting from the change from a doublet configuration for 5 increasing to a triplet configuration for 6. Oxidation of 5 ultimately leads to net Hatom abstraction at the NAd unit with reorganization of the F,tbsL ligand to accommodate the oxidized ortho-phenylenedianilido unit to its semiquinonate form (Figure 4). Delocalized radical character on the nitrenoid (NAd), anilido N from the ligand, and Ni, apparent in MO298, could account for the observed reactivity and tautomerization observed to form 7 or 8. Conclusions*

Herein we aimed to develop a trinuclear platform where redox activity is localized to a single metal site. Through a stepwise approach, we synthesized (F,tbsL)Zn2Ni(py) clusters which are capable of multi-electron chemistry despite the incorporation of redox-inactive Zn2+ centres into the trinuclear core. Using this platform, [Zn2Ni(μ3– NAd)]n (n = –1, –2) clusters were synthesized and fully characterized across two different oxidation states. X-ray absorption studies of the [Zn2Ni] nitrenoids indicate that the Ni centres in 5 and 6 are indistinguishable: the Ni–nitrenoid bond in 5 is best described as a Ni2+ with imidyl character, while the dianion is best described as a high-spin Ni2+ featuring an imido ligand. However, the DFT analysis suggest oxidation of 6 to 5 is primarily Ni-centred, favouring a NiIII imido formulation for 5. Future studies will involve characterizing the redox isomers using N K-edge XAS. Overall, the exact nature by which the Zn2+ cations are influencing the bonding of the MLMB unit is still under investigation. However, we note that forcing the nitrenoid ligand to act as a Lewis base serves to diminish its covalency to the redox-active Ni site. The Lewis base (NAd)-Lewis acid (Zn2+) interaction can stabilize the charged nitrenoid ligand electrostatically, but does not contribute to the canonical bonding (i.e., formal covalent bonding between the Zn–NAd). Terminal MLMBs between Ni–N feature short formal bonds given their combination of both σ and π bonding.[6;8] The long Ni–N bonds in both 5 and 6 suggest insignificant π overlap, reducing the formal bond order between the Ni and N. The

reduced formal bond order is further evidenced by the high spin electronic configuration observed for 6 whereas the majority of (Ni2+)(NR) complexes are low spin,[25;29-32] the lone exception’s electronic structure being mandated by symmetry.[28] While the geometrical configuration of the nitrenoid ligand to the [Zn2Ni] trinuclear plane is similar to related polynuclear nickel nitrenoid complexes,[38-39;45-46] the latter electronically saturate the nitrenoid valence shell to adopt imido (i.e., NR2–) character; whereas the nitrenoid ligands in 5 and 6 are far more electrophilic resulting from the lack of strong covalent bonding to the [Zn2Ni] core. The comparison of reactivity, bonding metrics, and hole character on the multiply bonded ligand between the [Zn2M(μ3–NAd)], [M2Zn(μ3–NAd)], and [M3(μ3–NAd)] clusters may yield insight into the exact role of the Zn2+ cations in metal-ligand bonding.

## Entry for the Table of Contents

Stepwise metalation of a polynucleating ligand generated heterobimetallic clusters featuring two redox inactive Lewis acids (Zn2+) and one transition metal (Ni). Reduction of the [Zn2Ni] cluster and reaction with a nitrene transfer reagent yielded [K(THF)3][(F,tbsL)Zn2Ni(μ3–NAd)]. Ni Kedge XAS (X-ray absorption spectroscopy) studies support the assignment of the primary redox pair as a divalent nickel coupled to an imidyl ligand.
